newsitem.title: USA: Aluminum market poised for higher prices - broker.
newsitem.headline: Aluminum market poised for higher prices - broker.

text.p: A tightening scrap market, rising U.S. Midwest premiums and funds holding large short positions in a relatively balanced market all point toward higher prices for aluminum next year, said Fred Demler, minerals economist at broker E D and F Man International.

Demler told delegates at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries round table here that destocking among aluminum consumers was coming to an end, the growth in aluminum production was slowing down along with east to west metal exports.
"It's been a fairly well balanced market over the last several months," Demler said. "The market is poised for a major rebound."

The average price in 1995 was 82 cents per pound, and forecast by Demler to fall to about 67 cents per pound this year after briefly dipping to a low of about 58 cents. The average price next year is forecast to rise to 69 cents.
But things could get worse before the get better.
"For the next one to two months, the sentiment is weak - the speculators are still short and they will be selling every rally," Demler said. "LME stocks are still high and building."
Russian sales were also up 10 percent on last year, and consumer buying has softened with scaling back of longer term hedging.
The bottom of the market will be reached in October to November, with the turnaround by the end of this year or early 1997.
"We could see a $200 to $300 per tonne move in price if the funds cover their short positions," Demler said.

Demler estimated that so-called stealth stocks or off- exchange stocks - not accounted for in any official figures totaled 300,000 to 600,000 tonnes but were tied up in financial arrangements and not freely available.
Shipments of aluminum rebounded 19 percent in July compared to January this year and International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) stocks, held by producers, were falling.

Although 1.1 million tonnes of idled capacity hangs over the market, about 900,000 tonnes is in the hands of just two major producers, Alcoa and Reynolds Metals. They would be reluctant to restart shuttered potlines at current prices, Demler said.
Demler forecast a market deficit of 100,000 tonnes in the second half of 1996, and a deficit of 280,000 tonnes in the first half of 1997.
Current aluminum inventories equal to 9.6 weeks of consumption, with equilibrium in the market at 7 to 9 weeks of consumption, Demler said.
